points-of-sail.title: Trim through the points of sail
points-of-sail.summary: Turn from close to the wind to a run, easing the sails as you go.
points-of-sail.see: You are sailing close to the wind (close-hauled) on starboard tack: the wind comes over the right side of the bow. The front edge of the mainsail is flapping.
points-of-sail.happening: A sail works like a wing only when the wind meets it at the right angle. As you turn away from the wind (bear away), the wind comes more from the side and then from behind, so each sail has to be let out further.
points-of-sail.action: Each time you bear away, ease (let out) the sheets: the main until it stops being stalled, the jib all the way on a reach. On a run, let the main right out.
points-of-sail.mistake: Turning away without easing: the sails stall (the air stops flowing smoothly over them), she heels and slows. Turning too far on a run: the wind gets behind the main and throws the boom across (an accidental gybe).
points-of-sail.done: You sailed every point of sail from close-hauled to a run. The rule: the further from the wind, the further out the sails.

close-hauled.goal: Close-hauled: haul the main in until it stops flapping.
close-hauled.how: In Ropes, tap − on Main sheet until it reads about 12 %. Watch the Sails section: both sails read Good when they are trimmed.

close-reach.goal: Close reach: turn 20° away from the wind, then ease the main.
close-reach.how: Open Steering (the Autopilot block) and tap −10 twice. Each tap turns her 10° to port (left), away from the wind, which comes over the starboard side. Then, in Ropes, ease Main sheet to about 25 %. With Realistic ropes the Autopilot is at the Helm station.

beam-reach.goal: Beam reach: wind from the side. Ease the main and let the jib sheet right out.
beam-reach.how: In Steering, tap −10 three more times. Then, in Ropes, ease Main sheet to about 50 % and Jib sheet to 100 %. On a reach the self-tacking jib (it changes sides by itself) cannot go out far enough to read Good: let its sheet right out.

broad-reach.goal: Broad reach: wind from behind the side. Let the main right out.
broad-reach.how: In Steering, tap −10 four more times. In Ropes, ease Main sheet to 85 % or more: the boom stops at the shrouds (the wires that hold the mast up), so the main cannot go further out.

run.goal: Run: wind from behind. Hold the course for 10 seconds without a gybe.
run.how: In Steering, tap −10 three more times, to about 165° from the wind. Do not go further: with the wind dead behind or on the other side, the boom can swing across by itself.

accidental-gybe.name: an accidental gybe
accidental-gybe.what: The boom swung across by itself (an accidental gybe).
accidental-gybe.why: The wind got behind the mainsail from the other side: she turned past dead downwind.
accidental-gybe.fix: The boom is now on the other side, so this step cannot pass from here. Tap 'Back to the start of step 5' and turn only three times this time.

by-the-lee.name: sailing by the lee
by-the-lee.what: You are sailing by the lee: the wind comes from the side the boom is on.
by-the-lee.why: She turned past dead downwind, so the boom can gybe at any moment.
by-the-lee.fix: Turn 10–20° back towards the wind straight away: tap +10 in Steering once or twice.

in-irons.name: stopping head to wind
in-irons.what: She has stopped, pointing into the wind (in irons).
in-irons.why: She turned towards the wind instead of away from it: no sail works with the wind straight ahead.
in-irons.fix: Turn away from the wind with −10 in Steering (Wind autopilot); if she does not answer, do the Getting out of irons exercise.

tacking.title: Tacking
tacking.summary: Turn the bow through the wind, first with the autopilot, then by hand.
tacking.see: You are sailing close-hauled on starboard tack: the wind comes over the right side of the bow.
tacking.happening: To reach a place upwind a sailing boat zigzags: she tacks (turns her bow through the wind) from one side to the other. The self-tacking jib changes sides by itself, so only the wheel is needed.
tacking.action: Turn steadily and keep turning until the wind is about 40° on the other side of the bow, then straighten up and let her speed up before you point higher.
tacking.mistake: Turning too slowly, or straightening up while the bow still points into the wind: she stops head to wind (in irons) and will not steer.
tacking.done: You tacked with the autopilot and by hand. Keep the wheel over until the wind is well on the new side, then let her speed up.

tack-autopilot.goal: Tack with the autopilot, then let her speed up to 4 knots.
tack-autopilot.how: In Steering, tap Tack. The autopilot turns her through the wind and holds the same angle on the other side. Wait until the speed on the strip reads 4 knots or more.

tack-by-hand.goal: Now tack back by hand: autopilot to Standby, wheel hard to port.
tack-by-hand.how: In Steering, tap Standby (the autopilot stops steering), then set Wheel to −25° (to port: the wind now comes from port, so port is towards it) and keep it there while the bow crosses the wind.

centre-wheel.goal: When the wind is 35° on the new side, centre the wheel.
centre-wheel.how: Watch the wind angle on the strip. When it reads about 35° from starboard, set Wheel to 0° in Steering. Centring earlier leaves her stuck head to wind.

pick-up-speed.goal: Sail close-hauled and let her speed up to 4 knots.
pick-up-speed.how: In Steering, tap Wind (it holds the angle she has now), then “10° to port” once, to about 45° from the wind. Both sails should read Good.

in-irons.name: stopping head to wind
in-irons.what: She has stopped head to wind (in irons).
in-irons.why: The turn was too slow, or the wheel came back to the centre before the bow was through the wind. With the wind straight ahead no sail works, and with no speed the rudder does nothing.
in-irons.fix: Ease both sheets, put the wheel hard over and wait while she drifts back: the Getting out of irons exercise shows how.

irons.title: Getting out of irons
irons.summary: She has stopped head to wind. Get her sailing again.
irons.see: The bow points straight into the wind. Both sails flap, she has no speed and the wheel does nothing.
irons.happening: With the wind straight ahead no sail can work (the no-go zone). The wind pushes her slowly backwards, and going backwards the rudder works the other way round: it turns the bow away from the wind.
irons.action: Let both sheets out, put the wheel hard over and hold it while she drifts back. When the wind is about 40° on the bow, centre the wheel and sheet in.
irons.mistake: Sheeting in hard, or waiting with the wheel in the middle: she stays head to wind.
irons.done: She is sailing again. Going backwards the rudder turns the bow the other way: hold the wheel over and be patient.

ease-sheets.goal: Let both sheets out to 40 % or more.
ease-sheets.how: In Ropes, set Main sheet and Jib sheet to about 60 %.

wheel-over.goal: Put the wheel hard over and wait until the wind is 35° or more on the bow.
wheel-over.how: In Steering, set Wheel to +30° and keep it there. She drifts backwards and the bow slowly falls away from the wind. This takes about a minute.

sail-away.goal: Centre the wheel, sheet in and sail away at 3 knots or more.
sail-away.how: In Steering, set Wheel to 0°. In Ropes, set Main sheet to about 12 % and Jib sheet to about 30 %. Both sails should read Good.

gybing.title: Gybing: controlled and accidental
gybing.summary: Turn the stern through the wind with the main hauled in, then see what an accidental gybe does.
gybing.see: You are on a run (the wind from behind) on starboard tack, with the main let right out.
gybing.happening: In a gybe the stern crosses the wind and the boom swings to the other side. With the main let out, the boom crosses the whole cockpit fast and stops with a bang. Hauled in first, it only moves a little.
gybing.action: Haul the main in until the boom is near the centre, turn until the wind is on the other side, then let the main out again.
gybing.mistake: Turning through the wind with the main still out, or steering past dead downwind without meaning to: the boom slams across (an accidental gybe). This boat has no preventer (a line that would hold the boom out).
gybing.done: A controlled gybe moves the boom a short way, slowly. An accidental one swings it across fast, with a big load on the main sheet and on anyone in its way. Haul in first.

haul-main.goal: Haul the main in until the boom is near the centre.
haul-main.how: In Ropes, set Main sheet to 5 %. The boom comes within 16° of the centre line.

gybe.goal: Gybe: turn until the wind is on the other side.
gybe.how: In Steering, tap Gybe (the Tack button reads Gybe on a run). She turns through the wind and the boom crosses a short way.

ease-main.goal: Let the main right out on the new side.
ease-main.how: In Ropes, set Main sheet to 85 % or more.

accidental.goal: Now see an accidental gybe on purpose: turn 30° further from the wind, past dead downwind.
accidental.how: In Steering, tap Heading, then “10° to starboard” three times: she turns from 15° short of dead downwind to 15° past it. The wind gets behind the main from the wrong side and throws the boom across. Watch the gybe report: the boom’s speed and the load on the main sheet.

accidental-gybe.name: an accidental gybe
accidental-gybe.what: The boom crossed by itself (an accidental gybe).
accidental-gybe.why: The main was still out when the stern crossed the wind, or she was steered past dead downwind.
accidental-gybe.fix: Haul the main in before you gybe. On a run keep the wind on the side away from the boom: never sail by the lee.

gusts.title: Gusts: ease the main
gusts.summary: Keep her upright through three gusts by easing the main.
gusts.see: You are on a close reach in 15 knots of wind with gusts. A gust shows on the water as a darker patch coming towards you.
gusts.happening: In a gust the wind is stronger for a few seconds: the sails push harder, she heels more and wants to turn into the wind (weather helm). Easing the main spills the extra wind.
gusts.action: When a gust hits, ease the main sheet by about 20 %; when it has passed, sheet in again.
gusts.mistake: Holding the main sheet tight in a gust: she heels past 25°, slows down and can turn into the wind by herself (a round-up).
gusts.done: Easing the main in a gust keeps her upright and steering. The dark patch on the water warns you a few seconds before it arrives.

three-gusts.goal: Get through three gusts: ease the main in each one, sheet in after.
three-gusts.how: Watch the strip: GUST shows while a gust blows (from about 16.5 knots). In Ropes, set Main sheet to about 45 % when it shows, and back to about 25 % when it has gone. Three strong gusts take about two and a half minutes.

trim-back.how: When GUST has gone from the strip, set Main sheet to about 25 % and Jib sheet to about 50 %. Both sails should read Good; ease the main again if a gust comes.

overpowered.name: heeling too far
overpowered.why: The main sheet was too tight for the wind: the sails pushed harder than the keel could hold her upright.
overpowered.fix: Ease the main sheet as soon as the gust hits; sheet in again when it has passed.

round-up.name: a round-up
round-up.what: She turned into the wind by herself (a round-up).
round-up.why: Too much heel with a tight main: the rudder lost its grip and the sails turned her into the wind.
round-up.fix: Ease the main straight away and she comes back under control. In the next gust, ease earlier.

reduce-sail.title: Too much wind: roll the sails in
reduce-sail.summary: In 22 knots, roll in part of the jib and the main until she sails upright.
reduce-sail.see: 22 knots of wind on a close reach. The main is eased until it flaps, to keep her upright; she heels about 20°.
reduce-sail.happening: With full sails she heels too much in this wind. On this boat both sails roll up (the jib round the forestay, the main into the mast), so making them smaller takes a minute and nobody has to go on deck.
reduce-sail.action: Ease the jib sheet and roll the jib in to about 40 %; roll the main in to about 60 %; then sheet the main in until it works.
reduce-sail.mistake: Pulling the jib in with its sheet still tight: the jib will not roll. And sails left flapping in strong wind wear out quickly.
reduce-sail.done: Smaller sails, less heel, and she sails almost as fast. Roll in early, before the wind gets up.

jib-in.goal: Roll the jib in to 45 % or less: ease its sheet first.
jib-in.how: In Ropes, set Jib sheet to 100 %, then Jib out to 40 %. Then set Jib sheet to about 75 % so the jib stops flapping. With the sheet tight the jib stops rolling.

main-in.goal: Roll the main in to between 50 and 65 %.
main-in.how: In Ropes, set Mainsail out to 60 %.

settle.goal: Sheet the main in until it reads Good, with less than 20° of heel.
settle.how: In Ropes, set Main sheet to about 35 % and hold it for 10 seconds. (A partly rolled jib reads Stalled in the app at any sheet: leave its sheet at about 75 %.)

overpowered.name: heeling too far
overpowered.why: Too much sail for this wind, or the main sheet pulled in too far.
overpowered.fix: Ease the main sheet now, then roll in more sail.

round-up.name: a round-up
round-up.what: She turned into the wind by herself (a round-up).
round-up.why: Too much heel: the rudder lost its grip and the sails turned her into the wind.
round-up.fix: Ease the main straight away, then roll in more sail.

sail-worn.name: a worn sail
sail-worn.what: A sail is worn from flapping.
sail-worn.why: A sail left flapping (flogging) in strong wind wears out fast.
sail-worn.fix: Sheet the flapping sail in until it stops, or roll it in.
